rows.label: P2
rows.article: The other one shows up when you get close

source.quote: Reactive protection often arrives when pain gets close. You suddenly want to drink, smoke, eat, scroll, text somebody, plan something, fix something, sleep, dissociate, get angry, or act out sexually.
source.from: the guide, Two Common Protective Patterns

rows.note: Your yawning angle: the yawn can bring an "I'm so done with this" feeling (the pull), and the yawn itself may be the opposite, since Re-evaluation Counseling counts yawning as emotional discharge (source: Wikipedia, Co-counselling). The tenth version; alone 100% Human, high. Two cold reads asked "the opposite of what?"; "the opposite of checking out" passes alone and waits for its context checks.

rows.label: P1
rows.article: Weeks in and nothing much is changing?

source.quote: If you keep trying something and not much seems to change, don’t immediately decide the whole method has failed—and don’t protect it by repeating the same thing forever either. First find out what actually happened.
source.from: the 2026-10-04 r4 guide, When to Change the Strategy

source.quote: Did you really get to the step you meant to practice, or did you mostly think, read, talk, or prepare for it? Was the adult function you needed actually available? Did fear, distrust, confusion, exhaustion, lack of skill, a practical barrier, or a protective part get in the way? If one concrete blockage shows up, work on that blockage and keep the larger goal.
source.from: the 2026-10-04 r4 guide, When to Change the Strategy

rows.note: Says it outright now: "Before either one, I'd look for what exactly is in the way" and "I'd work on that one thing instead of giving up on everything." Alone 100% Human, high, on the first try.

rows.label: P2
rows.article: Maybe you've been trying to comfort your little one

source.quote: For example, if you are trying to comfort the child but the loving adult position is not really there yet, the next move may be to borrow that adult function first—not to force more loving sentences at the child and not to declare reparenting useless. Then try the adjusted version and decide beforehand what small change would tell you it helped.
source.from: the 2026-10-04 r4 guide, When to Change the Strategy

rows.note: The example the right way round, "trying to comfort" while the loving grown-up isn't there yet. The hug picture went (it was the AI part). Alone 100% Human, high.

rows.label: P3
rows.article: One more thing about telling whether it helped.

source.quote: Match the claim to the duration. Ten minutes of relief followed by recurrence is ten minutes of relief, not evidence that the problem ended. If it helps, make one brief, bounded note of what changed, how quickly, how long it lasted, what returned, and what else was happening before deciding that the intervention caused the change or solved the underlying problem. Don’t turn outcome tracking into another checking ritual.
source.from: the 2026-10-04 r4 guide, When to Change the Strategy (new in r4; queue item PGQ-005)

rows.note: The duration point. Its "don't turn tracking into checking" is "and then leave it alone", since When Healing Turns Into Checking already says the rest. Eight versions failed alone; the plainest passed.

rows.label: P4

source.quote: Some effects should be visible quickly; others are skills that develop through repetition. Don’t invent a magic number of attempts. Change or stop the approach sooner when it is making things worse, you genuinely don’t want to do it, it is not feasible, the target turns out to be wrong, or something the method specifically predicted should happen keeps failing under the conditions where it was supposed to happen. A clearly better-supported route is also a reason to switch.
source.from: the 2026-10-04 r4 guide, When to Change the Strategy

source.quote: One more trap: don’t define “I did it correctly” as “it worked.” And don’t add a new invisible prerequisite every time it disappoints you. The point of reviewing the strategy is to learn what is actually helping, what is blocked, and what should change next—not to make the method impossible to disprove.
source.from: the 2026-10-04 r4 guide, When to Change the Strategy (the trap paragraph, cut; your sentences carry its point)

rows.note: Your three sentences, word for word, end it. "Can be a reason too" is "is a reason too" (a grounding: a settled no is enough). Alone 100% Human, high. Open: the last grounding wants "stopping counts" and "a no that's still there after you've heard it out is your answer"; both pass alone, but one put an AI window on that sentence in the section, and the API ran out before the rest.

rows.label: P5
rows.article: Sometimes the exercise is the part that works.

source.quote: Suggested reader-facing material to merge with that section without duplicating its existing strategy-review language: > There is another kind of mismatch to watch for: the inner-child exercise may actually go very well while ordinary life stays almost unchanged. You may find the child, feel real care, say exactly what needed to be said, and still return afterward to the same self-abandonment, hiding, chaos, or choices. > > That does not necessarily mean the meditation failed, and it does not necessarily mean you need a deeper or more powerful meditation. It may mean the missing step is transfer. > > Ask what the adult actually did in the exercise. Did they nurture, protect, guide, stay present, tell the truth, allow imperfection, or slow something down? Then choose one very small way—five percent is enough—to let that same function appear in ordinary life. > > The Nurturer might ask for support or let a safe person see something imperfect. The Protector might rest, set a boundary, leave an overwhelming situation, or stop using another person as a test. The Guide might choose one realistic next step instead of demanding certainty first. > > The child does not have to believe the new adult immediately. Words become more credible when ordinary life begins to match them. One small act of follow-through can sometimes teach more than repeating an already-successful meditation ten more times. > > Then review what happened without turning the review into another judgment of your worth. The question is simply whether this action made the caring, protective, or guiding function a little more real outside the exercise, and what should be kept or adjusted next time. Preserve these limits: do not require homework after every meditation; do not treat one outward act as generalized adult capacity; do not call weak carryover proof that the meditation was fake or that reparenting failed.

rows.label: PGQ-012 · Chicken-and-Egg, after the stages
rows.text: Whichever stage you're at, what you practice when you sit down with your little one has to make it out into the rest of your week sooner or later. Saying the right thing in there helps, but your little one really starts believing the grown-up you when that grown-up shows up on a regular Tuesday too, even in tiny ways.

source.quote: Suggested placement: immediately after the opening sequence that ends with “The adult and child in relationship.” Suggested reader-facing idea: > Each stage eventually has to leave the exercise. The inner adult becomes credible not only by saying the right thing in meditation, but by beginning to provide the same warmth, protection, or guidance in ordinary life—even in very small ways. Claude may humanize this freely; preserve the distinction between in-session capacity and ordinary-life transfer.

rows.note: Two review rounds; the second clean. Waits for Pangram.

rows.label: PGQ-001 · Catch the Hook
rows.text:
Feelings about yourself work the same way. "I feel attracted" or "I feel ashamed" is real as a feeling, but it doesn't settle who you are, or who you love. (If you don't want to be touched, though, say no now and work out what it means later. Same if something might be dangerous right now, or might be a medical warning sign: step away or get checked first.)

And there's the opposite mistake. If it's your orientation or your gender in question, I wouldn't write it off as "just an intrusive thought" only because it's unwanted, or because your family or church wouldn't like it. You don't have to decide either way today. And when tomorrow's feeling points the other way, I wouldn't let it, or anybody else, decide which one is the "real you." What you keep finding with real people, and in how you actually live, will tell you more over time than the loudest feeling of the hour.

source.quote: The same distinction applies inward. “I feel attraction,” “I feel aversion,” “I feel ashamed,” or “something feels wrong” reports an experience. It does not automatically prove who you are, what you want, whom you love, what is safe, or what you must do. A sensation can be completely real as a sensation and still need interpretation. That distinction never overrides consent, immediate danger, or possible medical red flags: take the cheap reversible precaution first—pause, leave, decline, or get checked—then interpret when it is safe to do so.
source.from: the r4 guide, Catch the Hook

source.quote: The opposite mistake matters too. Don’t dismiss your own genuine attraction, orientation, gender identity, or another meaningful part of your experience as “just intrusive” or “not the real you” merely because it is unwanted, stigmatized, confusing, or conflicts with personal, family, community, or religious expectations. You do not have to force a conclusion in either direction. Separate the experience itself from the meaning you are giving it and from the urge to get certainty right now, and let repeated real-life patterns show you more over time.

When the next sensation points the other way, don’t make somebody else, your body, or the strongest feeling of the hour decide which one is the “real you.” Notice the experience, keep the interpretation provisional, and let chosen action answer to evidence and values rather than whichever state is loudest.

rows.note: Three review rounds (consent and medical warning signs kept, orientation and gender named, no recurrence test). Waits for Pangram.

rows.label: PGQ-002/003 · Also Look Outward
rows.text:
Then there are people you're just getting to know. Meeting them can turn into a kind of test. If the real reason you're asking someone out is to prove you're lovable, or that you're sure what you want, then they've become part of the test. I'd lower the stakes. Get curious about them, and let them have their own reasons for being there. Can you just be with them without it turning into a verdict on you?

And being yourself with people doesn't mean telling strangers everything. Privacy isn't fakery. People can earn more of you by how they handle the smaller things you tell them, and how they take it when you say no. But if a relationship is getting deep and you're still keeping up a fake normal, happy version of yourself to hold onto it, I'd either bring more of the truth in, carefully, or let it be less deep for now. (If telling could put you in real danger, like violence, or being outed where that isn't safe, protect yourself first.) And when someone finally accepts you, it can feel amazing. It still doesn't prove they love you, or that they've earned your trust yet.

source.quote: Social practice can also become a performance test. If you are approaching people mainly to prove that you are normal, attractive, lovable, sexually or romantically certain, or capable of intimacy, the other person has become part of the test. Lower the stakes. Practice ordinary reciprocal contact: notice the other person, be curious, let them have their own purposes, and see whether you can be present without turning the interaction into a verdict on you.
source.from: the r4 guide, Also Look Outward

source.quote: Honesty does not mean total disclosure to strangers. Privacy is not fakery. Let people earn access by how they handle smaller truths, boundaries, and vulnerability. But if a relationship is becoming deep while you have to maintain a false normal, happy, or perfect persona to keep it going, either bring more truth in carefully or reduce the depth. Where honesty itself would expose you to coercion, violence, serious stigma, or another concrete danger, protect yourself first; authenticity is not a duty to disclose into an unsafe relationship. Another person is not a diagnostic instrument or reassurance machine. Healthy support and mutual co-regulation are part of relationships, and in a crisis getting a safe human involved can be exactly the right move. Relief at finally being accepted can be powerful; it is not by itself proof of romantic love, compatibility, or earned trust.

rows.note: Three review rounds. Waits for Pangram.

rows.label: PGQ-002 · When Healing Turns Into Checking
rows.text: Checking doesn't have to happen in your head, either. If you're going on a date mainly to prove you're normal, or that you're really attracted to someone, it's doing the same job as another hour of worrying. It might calm you down for a day, and then the next wobble feels even bigger. I'd only go when you'd want the company anyway, and drop the proving part. Bailing just to make the doubt go away can be the same checking from the other side. (Feeling unsafe is different, and so is touch or sex you want to stop. You're always allowed out of those.) Trying things out to find who you're attracted to isn't checking, either, as long as you're not grading every moment for a verdict. Ordinary life will show you more over time.

source.quote: A checking loop can move into behavior. Another body scan, conversation, confession, date, sexual encounter, search, or “exposure” can do the same job as another hour of rumination if the hidden demand is “prove I am normal,” “prove I am attracted,” “prove I can love,” “prove I am safe,” or “prove I am not bad.” The test may calm uncertainty briefly and then make the next fluctuation matter even more.
source.from: the r4 guide, When More Processing Becomes the Hook

source.quote: Do the action when it serves a life you actually choose—connection, curiosity, practice, work, play, kindness—not merely to force certainty. Avoidance can serve the same certainty loop from the other side. If you are doing exposure, including clinician-guided ERP, keep the useful exposure and drop the checking rather than fleeing the situation or escalating it into a bigger test. Exposure never requires continuing touch or sex you want to stop, staying in concrete danger, or skipping a check of a possible medical red flag. Exploring sexuality, orientation, gender, attraction, or relationship fit is not “checking” merely because the answer is uncertain; it becomes checking when the repetitive certainty-seeking pattern is actually there. If an answer genuinely needs time, let ordinary life and repeated patterns provide evidence without constantly monitoring them for a verdict.

rows.note: Three review rounds. Waits for Pangram.

rows.label: PGQ-004 · Start With Whatever Showed Up
rows.text: Anxiety deserves the same kind of listening, but it isn't a fortune teller. It might really be warning you about something, like being overloaded, or a boundary. In everyday decisions, I'd ask it what it's trying to protect, and then check what it predicted against what actually happens. Listening to it doesn't mean letting it drive. If you're actually in danger right now, though, get safe first, and get a possible medical warning sign checked instead of testing it. And some of what it says isn't a prediction at all. If a part of you is saying no to going deeper, or to an altered state, that's reason enough to stop, not something to test. With touch or sex, even a hesitation is enough.

source.quote: Anxiety deserves the same respect without becoming an oracle. It may be warning about overload, humiliation, danger, uncertainty, or a boundary. In ordinary-life decisions, hear the alarm, ask what it is trying to protect, and compare its prediction with evidence and what actually happens over time. But do not turn that into permission to push past a protector’s no to deeper processing or altered-state work, or past hesitation about touch or sex. Consent and immediate safety come first, and possible medical red flags get checked before they become psychological experiments. Listening to a protector is not the same as letting it drive; questioning a prediction is not the same as overriding a no.
source.from: the r4 guide, Start With Whatever Showed Up
